Robert Goddard. American physicist and engineer who pioneered liquid-fueled rocket propulsion and laid the theoretical and practical foundations of modern rocketry. Though largely dismissed by the American scientific establishment during his lifetime, Goddard's patents and designs became the blueprint for postwar rocket development.

In March 1926 in Auburn, Massachusetts, he launched the first liquid-fueled rocket — a modest ten-foot vehicle that rose forty-one feet. This proved the concept viable when nearly all experts thought it impossible. Goddard patented the multi-stage rocket concept in 1914 and the idea of using a nozzle to accelerate exhaust — foundational principles for all modern rocket engines.

He developed gyroscopic stabilization systems and vanes in the exhaust stream to steer rockets, solving the control problem that had stymied earlier attempts. His nineteen-nineteen paper A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes was ridiculed by the press as unscientific. The New York Times even published an editorial doubting he understood Newton's third law — they did not retract it until nineteen sixty-nine, after Apollo 11.

Goddard built high-altitude experimental rockets in Roswell, New Mexico, between nineteen thirty and nineteen forty-one, reaching altitudes above seven thousand feet and speeds exceeding the speed of sound. The U.S. Army Signal Corps and later NASA based early ballistic missile and space programs on Goddard's patents. He held two hundred and fourteen rocket-related patents.
